messages.content: What does AlphaFold's pLDDT measure, and why do design benchmarks such as RFdiffusion3 count a design as a success only when a structure predictor reproduces it confidently? Show the AlphaFold DB model of human histone H3.1 (UniProt P68431) coloured by pLDDT with the histone fold highlighted, and explain what the low-confidence tail means.

## What pLDDT measures

pLDDT is AlphaFold's per-residue self-assessment of local structural accuracy. The model is trained to predict, for each residue, the value of the **lDDT-Cα** score that its prediction would achieve against the (unseen) experimental structure. lDDT itself is a superposition-free measure: for a residue $i$, one takes all atom pairs $(i,j)$ whose true distance $d_{ij}^{\text{true}}$ falls inside an inclusion radius (15 Å), and asks what fraction of those distances is reproduced to within a tolerance:

$$\text{lDDT}_i=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\tau\in\{0.5,1,2,4\ \text{Å}\}}\frac{\big|\{j: |d_{ij}^{\text{pred}}-d_{ij}^{\text{true}}|<\tau\}\big|}{|\{j\}|}$$

AlphaFold emits this as a classification over 50 bins on $[0,100]$ and reports the expected value, so pLDDT is a calibrated *predicted* lDDT, not a probability of correctness and not a global quality score. Two consequences matter in practice. First, it is **local**: a protein can have every domain at pLDDT 95 while the relative domain placement is wrong — that failure mode is reported by PAE (predicted aligned error), not pLDDT. Second, it is a *distance-restraint satisfaction* measure, so regions whose conformation is not determined by the sequence score low by construction.

The conventional bands used by the AlphaFold DB are: >90 very high (backbone and generally side chains reliable), 70–90 confident (backbone reliable), 50–70 low (backbone topology only suggestive), <50 very low. Tunyasuvunakool et al. (2021, *Nature*, proteome-wide AlphaFold) showed that the <50 band is strongly enriched for intrinsic disorder, so pLDDT has become a de facto disorder predictor.

## Why design benchmarks score success by confident re-prediction

Generative backbone models such as RFdiffusion do not produce a sequence, and nothing in the diffusion process guarantees that the geometry they emit is one that any amino-acid sequence actually encodes. The standard remedy is the **self-consistency / in-silico designability** loop: diffuse a backbone (optionally conditioned on a motif or ligand), design sequences for it with ProteinMPNN or LigandMPNN, then *independently* fold those sequences with a structure predictor and ask whether the prediction returns to the designed geometry. A design counts as a success only if the predictor is both **confident** (pLDDT above ~80, interface PAE below ~10 Å where relevant) and **consistent** (backbone RMSD to the design typically <2 Å, motif or catalytic-atom RMSD <1–1.5 Å, ligand RMSD within a stated threshold).

[Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3](/paper/c7355659-26db-46f6-811a-9a04066d0d6a) follows exactly this protocol across every modality it benchmarks: binder designs are sequence-designed with ProteinMPNN and re-predicted with RF3 under confidence and structural cutoffs; small-molecule binder designs are scored by the fraction of designs AlphaFold3 recapitulates; enzyme designs from the M-CSA Atomic Motif Enzyme benchmark are scored on whether the catalytic residues are reproduced after refolding to within 1.25 Å (RFD3 beats RFD2 on 37 of 41 tasks); RNA puzzles are scored with pLDDT >0.9 and RMSD <4 Å thresholds. Its RNA-aptamer numbers also show how sharply the threshold choice matters — roughly 1% success at a 4 Å ligand-RMSD cut versus roughly 25% at 8 Å, with median inter-sample ligand RMSD around 3.4 Å.

The logic of the filter is that the predictor acts as a cheap, approximately orthogonal surrogate for the folding free-energy funnel. A sequence that folds confidently and uniquely to the intended backbone is one for which the designed structure is a deep, well-separated minimum; low pLDDT means the predictor found no single dominant conformation, which empirically correlates with soluble-but-molten or simply non-expressing designs. The filter is a strong enrichment step, not a proof: it is known to be gameable (predictors are biased toward idealised, hyperstable, helical de novo geometries and tend to be over-confident on them), it says nothing about kinetics or catalysis, and RFD3's own wet-lab numbers make the gap plain — 4 active designs out of 96 for the phosphotriesterase campaign (ZAPP-1, $k_{\text{cat}}=0.015\pm0.003$ s$^{-1}$), against 56 of 96 showing cleavage for the TTR protease (TTRg11, $k_{\text{cat}}/K_M = 1100\pm300$ M$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$). Confident re-prediction is necessary for a design to be worth testing, far from sufficient for it to work.

It is worth noting a conceptual tension the library flags: pLDDT is a property of the *predictor's* internal state, and recent interpretability work shows those states are not a transparent readout of physics. [Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1's trunk–diffusion boundary](/paper/f3c7e480-74ca-41ee-a913-7536162d9ce4) finds that a β-strand direction with F1 = 0.82 decodability in the trunk produced no measurable change in strand content when used to steer, and [How Do Co-folding Models Organize Structural Information?](/paper/88c0d7c6-c1ec-4b4e-a0a3-3107f9dc681e) shows the diffusion module reconciles intra- and inter-chain constraints the trunk leaves inconsistent. Confidence scores inherit whatever the trunk failed to resolve.

## Histone H3.1 coloured by pLDDT

```structure
{"title": "Human histone H3.1 (P68431), AlphaFold DB model coloured by pLDDT",
 "models": [{"afdb": "P68431", "color": "plddt"}],
 "highlights": [{"label": "N-terminal tail (1-44)", "resi": "1-44", "style": "sticks", "color": "grey"},
                {"label": "Histone fold alpha-N + alpha1", "resi": "45-77", "color": "accent"},
                {"label": "Histone fold alpha2 (long central helix)", "resi": "85-114", "color": "warm"},
                {"label": "Histone fold alpha3", "resi": "121-131", "color": "violet"}],
 "focus": "Histone fold alpha2 (long central helix)",
 "caption": "Blue = pLDDT > 90, cyan 70-90, yellow 50-70, orange < 50: the helix-strand-helix-strand-helix histone fold scores high, the ~40-residue N-terminal tail collapses into the very-low band."}
```

H3.1 is 136 residues. The AlphaFold model splits cleanly into two regimes. Residues ~45–135 form the canonical **histone fold** — a long central α2 helix of about 29 residues flanked by the shorter α1 and α3 helices, connected by the L1/L2 loops — and score in the confident-to-very-high bands. Residues 1–~40, the N-terminal tail that carries the H3K4/K9/K27/K36 methylation and acetylation marks, score very low, typically below 50, and are rendered as an extended, physically implausible-looking streamer.

## What the low-confidence tail means

The tail's low pLDDT is a correct prediction, not a failure. Three readings, in increasing order of usefulness:

**Geometric.** By the lDDT definition above, a residue scores high only if its distances to neighbours within 15 Å are reproducible. For a residue in a disordered tail there is no single set of such distances to reproduce, so no prediction can score well and the trained confidence head learns to say so. The splayed conformation rendered in the viewer is one arbitrary member of an ensemble, chosen essentially at random by the structure module; it should be read as "no defined position", never as an extended-chain model.

**Evolutionary/informational.** AlphaFold's intra-chain geometry is largely supplied by coevolutionary coupling in the MSA. [How Do Co-folding Models Organize Structural Information?](/paper/88c0d7c6-c1ec-4b4e-a0a3-3107f9dc681e) quantifies this for the Boltz-1 trunk: intra-chain distance content is MSA-saturated, reaching $R^2\approx0.3$ already at the Pairformer entry, whereas inter-chain content has to be built up across the 48 layers. Histone tails are among the most conserved sequences in biology but their conservation is functional (modification sites), not structural — there are no tertiary contacts to generate coupling signal, so the pair representation never acquires restraints for them.

**Biological and context-dependent.** The tail is genuinely intrinsically disordered as an isolated chain, which is what P68431's single-chain prediction models. It becomes ordered conditionally: it threads between the DNA gyres in the nucleosome and adopts defined conformations when bound by reader domains (chromodomains, bromodomains, PHD fingers). This is the key caveat for anyone using pLDDT in a design or annotation pipeline — low pLDDT means "not determined by this sequence in this context", which conflates genuine disorder, conditional folding, and missing context such as a binding partner, a ligand, or the rest of the complex. A single-chain AlphaFold DB entry cannot distinguish these. For the nucleosomal, ordered form you would need to predict or inspect the octamer with DNA.

The same ambiguity is why designability filters quote confidence *together with* an RMSD-to-target criterion rather than confidence alone, and why RFD3 conditions on the non-protein components of a system explicitly: a scaffold evaluated out of context inherits exactly the kind of context-dependent low confidence seen in the H3 tail.

## Further reading

- Jumper et al., "Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold", *Nature* 596 (2021) — the pLDDT head and its calibration.
- Mariani et al., "lDDT: a local superposition-free score", *Bioinformatics* 29 (2013) — the underlying metric.
- Tunyasuvunakool et al., *Nature* 596 (2021) — proteome-wide pLDDT and the disorder correspondence; Ruff & Pappu, *JMB* 433 (2021) for a critical view of AlphaFold on IDRs.
- Dauparas et al., "Robust deep learning–based protein sequence design with ProteinMPNN", *Science* 378 (2022), and Watson et al., *Nature* 620 (2023) — origin of the self-consistency designability protocol.
- [Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3](/paper/c7355659-26db-46f6-811a-9a04066d0d6a) for the current state of atomic-resolution functional-site benchmarks and their wet-lab follow-through.

spec.title: lDDT-Cα and pLDDT
spec.caption: pLDDT is AlphaFold's predicted per-residue lDDT-Cα, i.e. the expected fraction of local Cα distances it will get right, which is why design benchmarks use it as a confidence filter for self-consistency.

steps.explanation: For residue i, the neighbourhood consists of the Cα atoms within the 15 Å inclusion radius in the reference structure.
For each tolerance τ, take the fraction of those neighbour distances that the model reproduces within τ of the reference distance.
Averaging over the four tolerances (in Å) gives a superposition-free local score on a 0–1 scale, or 0–100 when scaled.
AlphaFold's head predicts a 50-bin classification over [0,100] for each residue, instead of a single number.
The reported pLDDT is the expected value of the predicted distribution, where c_b is the centre of bin b.

spec.title: AlphaFold DB pLDDT confidence bands
spec.caption: Width of each AlphaFold DB pLDDT band on the 0–100 axis: very low (<50, typically associated with intrinsic disorder), low (50–70), confident (70–90), very high (>90). Bar height is the band's width in pLDDT units.
spec.x_label: Confidence band (pLDDT range; <50 linked to intrinsic disorder)

spec.title: Self-consistency designability loop: design, refold, compare
spec.caption: A backbone from RFdiffusion gets a sequence from ProteinMPNN. A predictor (RF3 or AlphaFold3) refolds that sequence, and the prediction is overlaid on the design. Low pLDDT means the predictor is unsure the sequence encodes this fold. That shows up as a large deviation, a high PAE and a high RMSD.

c7355659-26db-46f6-811a-9a04066d0d6a.title: Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3
c7355659-26db-46f6-811a-9a04066d0d6a.summary:
## Contribution
RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) is a generative artificial intelligence framework for the de novo design of biopolymers (proteins and nucleic acids) at an all-atom resolution. Unlike its predecessors (RFdiffusion1 and 2), which primarily operate at the amino acid residue level, RFD3 enables precise atomic-level control over functional sites, such as enzyme active sites and ligand-binding pockets. This allows for the design of complex interactions with non-protein components (small molecules, RNA, and DNA) within a unified, multi-modal generative framework.

## Methods
RFD3 employs an all-atom diffusion process utilizing a transformer-based U-Net architecture. The architecture consists of three primary components: (i) a downsampling module for encoding atomic and residue-level features, (ii) a sparse transformer module for token-wise information processing using distance-based attention to focus on local interactions, and (iii) an upsampling module that uses cross-attention to modulate atomic features with token-level features to predict coordinate updates. …

f3c7e480-74ca-41ee-a913-7536162d9ce4.title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1’s trunk–diffusion boundary
f3c7e480-74ca-41ee-a913-7536162d9ce4.summary:
## Contribution
This paper investigates the representational shift of biological information as it moves from the representation-learning "trunk" to the coordinate-generating "diffusion" module in the Boltz-1 protein structure prediction model. The authors demonstrate that while the Pairformer trunk preserves both structural geometry and sequence chemistry, the diffusion module preserves geometry but significantly attenuates sequence chemistry. Furthermore, the study reveals that linear decodability of a feature does not guarantee causal steerability, specifically showing that highly predictive $\beta$-strand features in the trunk cannot be used to steer structure generation.

## Methods
The authors analyze per-residue activations from Boltz-1, extracting data from the 48-layer Pairformer trunk (every second layer) and the diffusion module (every second layer and every sampling step). They employ three primary analytical techniques:
1.  **Linear Probes:** Logistic regression probes trained on raw activations to measure decodability.
2.  **Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs):** TopK SAEs ($k=256$, 2048 latents) trained with $\ell_2$ regularization on demeaned activations to identify latent features. …

88c0d7c6-c1ec-4b4e-a0a3-3107f9dc681e.summary:
## Contribution
This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how co-folding models (specifically the Boltz-1 architecture) organize and evolve structural information within their internal representations. The authors move beyond single-chain analysis to investigate how multi-chain-specific representations—specifically the decomposition of the pair representation into intra-chain and inter-chain blocks—support joint biomolecular structure prediction. They identify three distinct information streams (single representation, intra-chain pair, and inter-chain pair) and characterize their functional roles, their evolutionary trajectory through the model depth (the "Mix–Compress–Refine" pattern), and the extent to which the diffusion module compensates for incomplete trunk representations.

## Methods
The researchers employ four distinct analytical "lenses" to study the Boltz-1 trunk:
1.  **Ablation (Interventional):** They apply zeroing, mean-only, and Gaussian (mean + variance) substitutions to the single representation ($S$), intra-chain pair ($Z_{intra}$), and inter-chain pair ($Z_{inter}$) blocks. This isolates whether the downstream diffusion module can still predict accurate structures when specific information streams are removed or randomized. …
